title: With all his might (2 Samuel 6:14–16)
hook: the king dances before the ark; Michal despises it

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. Your line was swifter than eagles. Today, the same man, his whole body full of joy.

Shouting. The blast of the shofar. A crowd pressing up the road into Jerusalem, and in the middle of it the ark of the covenant, carried up into the city. David is king now. He could ride beside it in robes, nodding to the crowd. Instead he's out in front of it, in the dust, dancing. Not a polite sway: the kind of dancing that makes people stare. And above the street, at a window, someone is watching. The same woman who once lowered him through a window to save his life.
screen: `SHOUTING AND THE SHOFAR.` → `THE ARK COMES TO JERUSALEM.` → `A FACE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might: in Hebrew, b'chol oz, with all strength. Nothing held back for his dignity. And he's not in the king's robes but a linen ephod, a simple garment the text gives to priests and to the boy Samuel serving at the shrine. Some translators render the dancing as whirling; the next verses add leaping. Then the camera moves to the window. Michal, the daughter of Saul, sees King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despises him in her heart. Notice how she's named: not David's wife, but the daughter of Saul, as if the old house is looking down at the new. When David comes home she meets him with sarcasm: how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself before the servants' maids. David answers that it was before the Lord he danced, and he'll be humbler still. Some readers hold this up as joy in God that doesn't stop to ask how it looks. Others make room for Michal's side. The woman at the first window gave everything for David. Between the two windows, the book has told us, Saul gave her to another man, and David later had her taken back while that husband walked behind her, weeping. It shows a king who forgot himself, and a woman who couldn't.
screen: `B'CHOL OZ: WITH ALL STRENGTH.` · `A LINEN EPHOD, NOT ROBES.` · `MICHAL DESPISES HIM.` · then, large: `WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.` · then: `BEFORE THE LORD I DANCED.`

segments.voice: If you're somewhere private, stand; if not, or you can't stand, you can do this sitting: shoulders, hands, head. Put on a song, in your head or out loud, something that makes you glad, and move to it with all your might, not well and not for anyone. If you pray, you can let the movement be your prayer.
b'chol oz. The Hebrew for with all strength, how David danced before the ark in a linen garment, holding nothing back. Today's word.
Your line: holding nothing back. Joy doesn't have to check who's watching first. More tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read David's dance before the ark in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and dancing with joy in worship carries on in Jewish life, as when people dance with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah.

chat.says: Why did David dance so wildly in the street? Isn't that strange for a king?
options: He danced before the Lord with all his might, holding nothing back.
He was showing off his royal robes so the crowd would admire him.
Michal had asked him to dance, so he did it to make her happy.
chat.meaning: The verse says David danced before the Lord b'chol oz, with all his might, in a simple linen ephod, not royal robes.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of 2 Samuel 6:14 (certain in the KJV).
'Some translators render his dancing as whirling' refers to the Hebrew mekharker; confirm.
Linen ephod on the boy Samuel is 1 Samuel 2:18; 'the kind the text gives to priests' also leans on 1 Samuel 22:18. Confirm.
Descriptions of the ark's contents were cut under the claims rule.
'Daughter of Saul ... the old house looking down on the new one' is a reading; confirm it is fair.
Michal's words and David's reply (6:20–22) are paraphrased; 6:23 is left out.
Simchat Torah dancing in howItsDone; confirm phrasing.
Editor: 'the girl at the first window' changed to 'the woman' (Michal was already David's wife in 1 Samuel 19), and the practice no longer tells the listener what voice they hear.

Audit: replaced 'the text doesn't tell us everything that happened between those two windows' with what the text does tell: Michal given to Palti (1 Samuel 25:44) and taken back by David's demand while her husband followed weeping (2 Samuel 3:14–16). This gives Michal's side its basis instead of leaving it vague.
